title: Count Negative Numbers in a Sorted Matrix
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every cell versus a staircase two-pointer walk exploiting the doubly-sorted structure.

content.title: Count Negative Numbers in a Sorted Matrix

blocks.text: Given an m x n integer matrix grid, sorted in non-increasing order both row-wise (left to right) and column-wise (top to bottom), return the total count of negative numbers in grid.

blocks.caption: Walk a staircase path from the bottom-left corner, exploiting the sorted structure

blocks.text: Given a matrix sorted in non-increasing order along both rows and columns, count how many of its entries are negative.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Waterline on a Sloped, Sorted Terrain
blocks.text: Like standing at the bottom-left corner of a terrain map where elevation only ever decreases moving right or moving up (equivalently, values only decrease moving right or down in the grid), and wanting to count every point below sea level (negative). Starting from the bottom-left and always stepping either up (when the current point is underwater, since everything further right on this row must be underwater too) or right (when the current point is above water, needing to search further right for where the water starts) traces out exactly the underwater/above-water boundary in one continuous walk.

blocks.caption: Each step either counts an entire row-stretch at once, or narrows the search by one column

blocks.text: Before checking every cell individually, notice that the sorted structure guarantees an entire stretch of cells is negative once just one boundary cell is found to be negative.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since every row is sorted in non-increasing order (left to right), the moment a cell is found to be negative, every cell to its right in that same row must also be negative (or equally negative), since values can only decrease or stay the same moving right.

Observation 2: Since every column is sorted in non-increasing order (top to bottom), a similar guarantee holds vertically.

Observation 3: Starting at the bottom-left corner and using two pointers (one for row, one for column), a "staircase" walk can be used: if the current cell is negative, the ENTIRE remainder of this row (from the current column to the end) is negative, so add that count directly and move UP a row (checking the same column, since the row above could have its own, possibly later, negative boundary); if the current cell is NOT negative, move RIGHT one column, since this cell and everything to its left in this row are confirmed non-negative, but the boundary might still be further right.

Observation 4: This walk terminates once either pointer runs off the matrix, having visited each row and column boundary at most once.

Recognizing that the "doubly sorted" structure lets an entire stretch of cells be confirmed at once (rather than needing to check each individually) is the key insight that turns an O(m*n) full scan into an O(m+n) staircase walk.

This is a two-pointer "staircase" walk, exploiting a matrix sorted along two axes simultaneously, similar in spirit to the classic search technique used in Search a 2D Matrix II elsewhere in this category.
Check every single cell in the matrix directly, counting how many are negative.

items: Iterate over every row and every column of the matrix.
For every cell, check whether it is negative, incrementing the count if so.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every cell is visited exactly once, using a straightforward nested loop, since this brute force does not yet exploit the sorted structure at all.
The check val < 0 is applied identically to every cell, regardless of its position.
count simply accumulates every negative cell found, in any order.

blocks.text: Every cell is checked directly, so the correct total count is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m * n), visiting every cell exactly once.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: checking every cell individually ignores that the matrix being sorted along BOTH rows and columns guarantees entire stretches of cells can be confirmed negative (or non-negative) at once, without needing to check each one.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force checks every cell individually. Instead, start at the bottom-left corner and use two pointers (row, col). Whenever the current cell is negative, the entire rest of that row (from col to n-1) is guaranteed negative too, so add that count directly and move up a row. Whenever the current cell is non-negative, move right one column to continue searching for where negatives begin in this row. This walk visits at most m + n cells total, far fewer than the full m * n grid.

Start with row = m - 1 and col = 0. While both pointers remain in bounds: if grid[row][col] is negative, add (n - col) to the count and decrement row; otherwise, increment col. Return the accumulated count once either pointer exits the matrix.
Walk a staircase path from the bottom-left corner, counting entire row-stretches at once whenever a negative boundary is found.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The pointer exits the matrix (row becomes -1), giving a final count of 8, matching the expected answer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m + n), since row only ever decreases and col only ever increases, together moving at most m + n times total.
Space: O(1) extra.

Because every row is non-increasing left to right, the moment grid[row][col] is negative, every cell from col to n-1 in that row must also be negative (or equal, but since it's already negative, still negative), so their count can be added directly without individually checking them. Moving up after counting a row's negative stretch is safe because the row above, being non-increasing top to bottom in every column, could have its own negative boundary at the same or a LATER column, never an earlier one, so nothing is missed by continuing from the same column pointer.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["grid[row][col] < 0","Every cell from col to n-1 in this row is negative; add (n - col) to the count and move up a row"],["grid[row][col] >= 0","This cell (and everything to its left in this row) is confirmed non-negative; move right to continue searching"]]}

items: Starting at the bottom-left corner ensures the walk begins where negatives are most likely (the smallest values in the matrix cluster toward the bottom-left, given the non-increasing row/column ordering).
row only ever decreases and col only ever increases, so the total number of steps is bounded by m + n, never more.
The count update (n - col) directly computes the size of the remaining negative stretch in a single arithmetic operation, without an inner loop.

blocks.text: When a grid is sorted along both axes simultaneously, a single "staircase" pointer walk from one corner can eliminate entire rows or columns' worth of cells at each step, turning an O(m*n) full scan into an O(m+n) walk.

items: Starting from the wrong corner (e.g., top-left), which doesn't allow the same clean "count and move" logic given a non-increasing sort order in both directions.
Moving in the wrong direction after a negative/non-negative check (e.g., moving right instead of up after finding a negative), which would recheck cells or skip valid ones.
Forgetting that the count added on a negative cell is (n - col), the full remaining row-stretch, not just 1 for the current cell alone.

items: Explicitly justify why starting at the bottom-left corner (rather than any other corner) is the natural starting point, given the specific non-increasing sort directions, since this choice (and its correctness) is exactly what an interviewer wants to see reasoned through.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Matrix sorted along BOTH rows and columns, count/find something" points toward a staircase two-pointer walk from an appropriate corner, eliminating entire rows or columns at each step rather than scanning every cell.

items: How would you solve this using binary search instead? For each row, binary search for the first negative value (since each row alone is sorted), summing (n - foundIndex) per row, giving O(m log n) time, slower than the O(m+n) staircase for large matrices but sometimes clearer to reason about.

How would this generalize to counting values ABOVE some arbitrary threshold, not just below 0? The exact same staircase technique applies directly, just replacing the "< 0" check with "< threshold" (or the appropriate comparison for the sort direction).

What if the matrix were sorted in NON-DECREASING order instead? The starting corner and movement directions would need to mirror accordingly (e.g., starting from the top-right corner instead), but the same staircase principle still applies.
The staircase two-pointer walk technique, also used in Search a 2D Matrix II elsewhere in this category, exploiting a matrix sorted along two axes to eliminate entire rows or columns per step.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(m * n) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (staircase walk): O(m + n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Staircase two-pointer walk from the bottom-left corner, exploiting a doubly-sorted matrix
Core Idea: A negative cell confirms its entire row-stretch negative at once; a non-negative cell narrows the search rightward
Time: O(m + n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: A matrix sorted along both rows and columns lets an entire row-stretch be confirmed negative in O(1), rather than checking each cell
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: From the bottom-left, negative means count (n-col) and go up; non-negative means go right
